passage:
"Whoa, it fell again," said Farhan.
"I hate this!" Arohi swept an arm across the mat and sent every block skidding.
"Hey, my foot!"
"Stupid tower!" Arohi's voice cracked.
"You got it up to six last time."
"Don't care." Arohi crossed both arms and stared at the wall.
Farhan sighed, Arohi's big brother, and began collecting the blocks.

qa.q: What did Arohi do with the blocks after the tower fell?
qa.a: Arohi swept an arm across the mat and sent every block skidding.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when saying "I hate this"?
qa.a: Arohi was angry and disappointed, with a cracking voice that shows the feeling was bigger than the block problem.

qa.q: What could Arohi try after calming down, and why?
qa.a: Arohi could rebuild with a wider base of the long blocks, because the earlier tries had shown what nearly worked, and calm helps to use it.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Arohi's outburst?
qa.a: Farhan is a bit surprised and hurt by the flying blocks, but he stays patient and begins to tidy up rather than scold.

grounding: When the tower falls a fourth time, a child sweeps the blocks off the mat and says "I hate this," so feelings run ahead of thinking.

passage:
Preschool note for Farhan's mother, Sangeeta
Farhan built his tower four times today. On the fourth fall he swept every block off the rug with his arm and said, "I hate this." He turned his back and folded his arms. I sat near him without talking for a while. Later we looked at the blocks together; he said the second tower had been the tallest, but he didn't want to try again today.

qa.q: What did Farhan say when he swept the blocks off?
What was Farhan feeling when he folded his arms?
qa.a: He was angry and discouraged after four falls.

qa.q: What would you advise for next time?
qa.a: Take a break after the second or third fall to calm down and look at what worked, like his second tower, before anger wipes the learning.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading this note?
qa.a: Sangeeta would likely feel sympathetic, and glad that someone sat with him calmly.

grounding: A preschool note describes a child who sweeps away his blocks in anger after the fourth fall, losing what earlier tries taught him.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the house in Shimoga as Hemant built his tower for the fourth time. His cousin Vaibhav watched. Three blocks, four, five, and down it went. Hemant's face went hot. He swept his arm across the mat and blocks flew into the corner. "I hate this!" He stomped to the door. Vaibhav said quietly, "Your third one was so tall, though."

qa.q: What did Hemant's cousin say quietly?
qa.a: He said, "Your third one was so tall, though."

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when his face went hot?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated after the tower fell for the fourth time.

qa.q: What could Hemant try instead of sweeping the blocks away?
qa.a: He could take a breath and look at what made the third tower tall, so the next try builds on that.

qa.q: How does the outburst look to Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav stays calm and wants to help, reminding Hemant of what worked.

grounding: A child sweeps away his blocks in anger after the fourth fall, and the learning from earlier towers is lost.
